title: How To Handle Your Students' Smart Phone Withdrawal
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that constant smartphone stimulation has eroded students' capacity for sustained academic effort, leaving them restless and unable to concentrate once devices are put away for class -- a state he frames explicitly as withdrawal. He criticizes the common teacher response to this problem, which has been to shorten and gamify instruction (short excerpts instead of full texts, more video and interactive technology, far lighter independent practice loads than in prior decades), arguing this accommodation has let students advance through school with weak reading and writing skills. His counter-proposal is deliberately contrarian: rather than competing with phones for stimulation, teachers should slow down, deliver genuinely great lessons, push harder on independent work, and trust that rebuilding real academic stamina is more rewarding to students than the alternative, even if it doesn't feel that way to them at first. He insists this doesn't require eliminating phone use altogether, only reasserting that phones have a place, not a monopoly, and closes with a call for teachers to be bold about holding this line rather than apologizing for high standards.
points: Constant phone stimulation has produced real withdrawal symptoms in students once devices are removed for instruction -- restlessness and an inability to concentrate for more than a few minutes.
Diagnoses the common teacher accommodation (shorter texts, more video, lighter homework loads) as a mistake that has let weak reading and writing skills slide through the grading system.
Prescribes the opposite of accommodation: slow down, deliver denser and clearer lessons, and push for more independent work rather than less.
The goal isn't eliminating phones but restoring students' understanding that academic depth and purpose are more meaningful than constant digital stimulation.
quotes: Since the advent of the smart phone, interest in acquiring academic skill and knowledge has dwindled.
Kids spend hour upon hour scrolling hits of dopamine and it’s crushed their desire to learn. Even worse, once their phones are put away for class, they go through withdrawal.
Great literature has been replaced with short articles and excerpts. Lessons are brief and include video, images, and interactive technology. Laptops are rarely out of sight and loosely monitored.
This has allowed students to skate by from one grade to the next, and even earn high marks with absurdly poor reading and writing skills.
Instead of shortening and increasing stimulation, we believe in doing the opposite: Slow down, provide great lessons, push the envelop on independent work, and heal their damaged brains.
Students appreciate and do better in a serious academic environment that will challenge them rather than one that capitulates to the jump-cut entertainment world and toxicity of social media.
